decisions.location: Experiment 1, p. 56 (line 229); Experiment 1 Discussion, p. 58 (line 361); Experiment 2 Discussion, p. 61 (line 559); General discussion, pp. 61-62 (lines 569, 575); References, p. 62 (line 579)
decisions.quote: Experiment 1 was designed to replicate the counteracting effect of sugar consumption on ego depletion (Gailliot et al., 2007; Hagger et al., 2010). Following the protocol of Wang and Dvorak (2010), participants’ delay-discounting rates were assessed prior and after the consumption of a sweet drink containing either sugar or artiﬁcial sweetener.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent for this work. Both Experiment 1 and Experiment 2 (via the DG glucose-ingestion vs. SS stevia-rinse contrast on go/no-go performance, which does not use Wang and Dvorak's protocol) directly retest Gailliot et al. (2007) on whether glucose consumption counteracts ego depletion (and Experiment 1 additionally retests whether performing a self-control task lowers blood glucose levels as reported by Gailliot et al., 2007). The reference list explicitly identifies Gailliot et al. (2007), 'Self-control relies on glucose as a limited energy source. Willpower is more than a metaphor,' Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 92(2), 325-336 (DOI: 10.1037/0022-3514.92.2.325). This target is a separate work from the sole shipped row (input_row_index 2004: Wang & Dvorak, 2010, Psychological Science, DOI: 10.1177/0956797609358096) and from sibling targets 2, 3, and 4.

corrected_value.title: The sweet taste of success. The presence of glucose in the oral cavity moderates the depletion of self-control resources.

decisions.location: Experiment 2, p. 58 (lines 367, 371); Experiment 2 Discussion, p. 61 (line 567); General discussion, pp. 61-62 (lines 569, 575); References, p. 62 (line 579)
decisions.quote: Rinsing one’s mouth with glucose solution did not signiﬁcantly alter ego depletion, neither when the solution was provided directly after the depletion task (reward drink), nor when it was provided directly before the second self-control task (signal drink). Hence, this experiment did not generate any evidence that sensing glucose in the oral cavity serves one of the two hypothesized psychological functions. Importantly, this implies that, despite applying a powerful research design, the present study could not replicate the ﬁndings presented by Hagger and Chatzisarantis (2012), Molden et al. (2012) and Sanders et al. (2012).
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent for this work. Experiment 2 directly retests the effect of oral glucose sensing (mouth rinsing with an 18% glucose solution vs. non-caloric sweetener for 10 seconds, measuring liquid volume before and after rinsing following Hagger & Chatzisarantis, 2012) on ego depletion, and explicitly concludes that it failed to replicate Hagger and Chatzisarantis (2012). The reference list identifies Hagger, M. S., & Chatzisarantis, N. L. (2012), 'The sweet taste of success. The presence of glucose in the oral cavity moderates the depletion of self-control resources,' Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 39(1), 28-42 (DOI: 10.1177/0146167212459912). This is a distinct work from shipped row 2004 (Wang & Dvorak, 2010) and from sibling targets 0, 3, and 4.

decisions.quote: The present study was designed to comply with the widespread call for replications by applying study protocols reported to results in substantial effects of sugar consumption (Gailliot et al., 2007; Wang & Dvorak, 2010) and sugar sensing (Hagger & Chatzisarantis, 2012; Molden et al., 2012) on ego depletion. (2012), 'The motivational versus metabolic effects of carbohydrates on self-control,' Psychological Science, 23, 1130-1137 (DOI: 10.1177/0956797612439069). corrected_value.title: Modelling learning from errors in daily work.

decisions.quote: The goal of our study was to investigate whether exploratory findings from an earlier study on hospital nurses’ ESLA (Bauer and Mulder Learning in Health and Social Care 6:121–133, 2011) replicate and generalise to the domain of elder care nursing. For this purpose, we surveyed a sample of N = 180 elder care nurses using vignette-based questionnaires. With these data, we tested a mediation model of nurses’ ESLA suggested by the earlier study.
decisions.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent for this work. In the abstract, the authors explicitly state that their survey of N = 180 elder care nurses tests whether exploratory mediation model findings from an earlier study on hospital nurses' engagement in social learning activities (ESLA) cited as 'Bauer and Mulder Learning in Health and Social Care 6:121–133, 2011' replicate and generalise to elder care nursing, and conclude that their results 'entirely cross-validate the exploratory findings of Bauer and Mulder (Learning in Health and Social Care 6:121–133, 2011)'. In the reference list, the exact journal, volume, and page range (Learning in Health and Social Care, 6, 121–133) uniquely match Bauer, J., & Mulder, R. H. (2007), 'Modelling learning from errors in daily work' (line 94; the 2011 year in the inline Springer abstract citation is a print conflation with a different 2011 article in Journal of Education and Work). Regardless, the sole shipped row (input_row_index 12) is a 2012 edited book chapter by Bauer, Gartmeier, and Harteis ('Human fallibility and learning from errors at work', DOI: 10.1007/978-90-481-3941-5_10), which is a completely different work from Bauer and Mulder's hospital-nurse study.
